task_row_model.query: Provide a cancellation-safe asyncio TCP client pattern that enforces a connection timeout and always closes the StreamWriter. Explain why close and wait_closed are necessary and when to use asyncio.shield.

documents.content: In asynchronous networking tutorials, asyncio.open_connection is the usual high-level API to create a TCP client: it returns a (StreamReader, StreamWriter) pair. To enforce a timeout on the connection phase, authors commonly wrap the coroutine in asyncio.wait_for(timeout=...). wait_for raises asyncio.TimeoutError on expiry and cancels the wrapped coroutine; the underlying connection coroutine may be interrupted mid-operation. Because StreamWriter.close() merely requests shutdown and the actual transport closure is asynchronous, you should call writer.close() and then await writer.wait_closed() to ensure the socket and transport are fully released. Failure to await wait_closed can leave resources held until garbage collection or program exit.
documents.reasoning_trace: Identified that open_connection returns reader/writer; wait_for enforces timeout and cancels the coroutine; close() is cooperative and wait_closed() must be awaited to fully release transport. These facts supply timeout mechanism and necessity to await wait_closed.

documents.content: Field notes from production teams report a recurrent leak when cancellation happens during writer.drain(): the transport can be left open if the coroutine is cancelled before shutdown completes. Practical guidance: wrap critical I/O shutdown in try/except CancelledError and ensure writer.close() is invoked in a finally block. Some teams use asyncio.shield around the shutdown await (for example, await asyncio.shield(writer.wait_closed())) so that a higher-level cancellation doesn't abort the cleanup; shielding prevents immediate cancellation of that await but also delays responding to cancellation, so use it sparingly for small, guaranteed-cleanup waits.
documents.reasoning_trace: This document provides the cancellation-during-drain leak scenario and recommends ensuring writer.close() in finally and optionally wrapping wait_closed in asyncio.shield to protect cleanup from external cancellation.

documents.content: Developer notes: implement the connect as a task and apply asyncio.wait_for to that task to impose a timeout. If wait_for raises TimeoutError, cancel the connect task (task.cancel()) and then check whether a StreamWriter was created; if so, call writer.close() and await writer.wait_closed() in a finally block. A pattern: create_task(asyncio.open_connection(...)), then try: reader, writer = await asyncio.wait_for(task, timeout); except asyncio.TimeoutError: task.cancel(); finally: if writer is not None: writer.close(); await writer.wait_closed(). Anecdotes and background on TCP stacks are irrelevant to the mechanics but often appear in posts.
documents.reasoning_trace: Gives an explicit coding pattern: run open_connection as a task, wrap with wait_for, cancel on TimeoutError, then ensure writer.close() and await wait_closed() in finally. This fills in the procedure for implementing timeout and cleanup.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Run asyncio.open_connection inside a task and enforce a timeout with asyncio.wait_for; if wait_for raises asyncio.TimeoutError, cancel the connect task. If a StreamWriter was created, always call writer.close() and await writer.wait_closed() in a finally block to fully release the transport. Wrap the wait_closed await with asyncio.shield if you must protect the cleanup from outer cancellation, but use shielding sparingly.
